definition: Cleaning, transforming, and organizing raw records so a mining algorithm can use them reliably.
wrongs: Grouping unlabeled records so members of each group are more similar to each other.
Scoring a finished model only on rows that were held out from fitting.
Listing item pairs that co-occur above a minimum basket frequency.
why: Models expect consistent, usable fields, so cleaning and transforming records is the preparation step before mining.
example: A clinic rescales lab units and fills blank glucose cells before training a readmission model.
scenario: A loan file mixes date formats, duplicate customers, and blank incomes. Which step should happen before any model is fit?
scenarioWhy: Inconsistent and incomplete fields have to be repaired and standardized before training can be trusted.

definition: Predicting a discrete category for a new record from examples whose categories are already known.
wrongs: Predicting a continuous number such as a sale price from labeled history.
Partitioning customers into similar groups when no group label exists.
Replacing each missing numeric cell with the median of its column.
why: The target is a known class, and the model learns that class from labeled examples.
example: A mailbox assigns each incoming message to spam or not spam using messages labeled last year.
scenario: A hospital must mark new lab panels as diabetic or not diabetic using past panels that already have diagnoses. Which task is this?
scenarioWhy: The diagnosis is a discrete label already present on the training panels, so the task is classification.

definition: Dividing unlabeled records into groups whose members are more similar to each other than to other groups.
wrongs: Assigning a predefined class to a record by using a labeled training set.
Counting correct and incorrect class predictions in a four-cell table.
Encoding each city name as its own binary column.
why: No target label is supplied, so groups are formed from similarity alone.
example: An online shop groups visitors by pages viewed without using any predefined segment names.
scenario: A telecom has call records but no customer-segment labels and wants sets of similar subscribers. Which task fits?
scenarioWhy: Similar subscribers must be grouped without a supplied label, which is clustering.

definition: An if-then pattern stating that when one itemset occurs, another tends to occur, with support and confidence.
wrongs: A node test that sends records down branches until a leaf predicts a class.
A center point that each assigned record is closer to than to other centers.
A curve of catch rate versus false-alarm rate as a threshold moves.
why: The pattern links a condition itemset to a result itemset and is accepted only when support and confidence are high enough.
example: A grocer learns that baskets containing diapers also often contain baby wipes.
scenario: A supermarket wants rules of the form if cereal is bought then milk is bought. Which pattern type is that?
scenarioWhy: The requested if-then link between items in a basket is an association rule.

definition: A classifier that tests one attribute at each internal node and assigns a class label at each leaf.
wrongs: A set of centers updated by the mean of the points assigned to each center.
A table whose cells count actual classes against predicted classes.
A code that gives shorter bit strings to more frequent symbols.
why: Each internal test routes a record, and the leaf that is reached supplies the predicted class.
example: A credit model asks about income, then about missed payments, and a leaf predicts default or not.
scenario: A student builds a model that asks yes-or-no questions about attributes and ends at a class label. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: Sequential attribute tests that end in class leaves are the structure of a decision tree.

definition: A clustering method that assigns each point to the nearest of k centers and updates those centers until they settle.
wrongs: A classifier that copies the majority class among the k nearest labeled neighbors.
A tree grown by always splitting on the attribute with lowest impurity.
A miner that keeps itemsets only when every subset is frequent.
why: The algorithm alternates nearest-center assignment and center updates, and k is chosen before the run.
example: A carrier splits 20000 subscribers into 4 groups by minutes, data use, and monthly bill.
scenario: An analyst must form exactly 5 unlabeled customer groups by minimizing distance to group centers. Which algorithm applies?
scenarioWhy: A chosen number of groups updated from nearest-center membership is k-means, not a labeled classifier.

definition: Judging how well a trained model predicts on records that were not used to fit it.
wrongs: Filling empty fields and removing duplicate rows before any algorithm runs.
Merging two frequent itemsets into a longer candidate itemset.
Moving cluster centers to the mean of their currently assigned points.
why: Performance on unseen records estimates generalization, which is the point of evaluating a mined model.
example: A team fits a churn model on 2022 accounts and scores it on 2023 accounts.
scenario: After fitting a donor model on last year's appeals, a charity checks predictions on this year's labeled appeals. What activity is that check?
scenarioWhy: Comparing predictions with labels on data kept out of fitting is model evaluation.

definition: Matching training records, including their noise, so closely that accuracy falls on new records.
wrongs: Using a model so simple that error stays high on both training and new records.
Holding out a single test slice and never training on it.
Stopping k-means when centers move less than a set distance.
why: The model has memorized sample quirks, so the training fit does not carry over to new data.
example: A deep tree labels every past student exam perfectly but misses many students in the next term.
scenario: A fraud tree is perfect on the training month and much worse on the next month. Which problem occurred?
scenarioWhy: Excellent training accuracy that collapses on later data is the usual sign of overfitting.

definition: A table of counts for every pair of actual class and predicted class.
wrongs: A ranked list of attributes ordered by information gain.
A plot of within-cluster distance against the number of clusters.
A list of store items sorted only by shelf price.
why: Each cell records how often a particular true class received a particular predicted class.
example: Of 50 diseased patients, 40 were flagged diseased and 10 were missed, and those counts sit in a class table.
scenario: A grader wants the counts of true spam, missed spam, false alarms, and correct ham in one table. Which display is that?
scenarioWhy: Those four counts are the cells of a two-class confusion matrix.

definition: Choosing a subset of the original input attributes and dropping the rest to simplify or improve a model.
wrongs: Building new attributes by combining every pair of original columns.
Labeling every row with the most common class in the whole file.
Storing each basket as a bitmap of every product in the catalog.
why: Selection keeps some existing attributes and discards others rather than inventing new coordinates.
example: A gene study keeps 30 markers out of 20000 measurements before building a tumor classifier.
scenario: A text model starts with 100000 word counts and keeps only 2000 informative words. Which step is that?
scenarioWhy: Keeping a subset of existing word attributes and dropping the rest is feature selection.

definition: Rotating which fold is tested so each record is used for testing in exactly one round.
wrongs: Training once on every row and reporting accuracy on those same rows.
Sorting records by the label before taking a single cut.
Deleting every column that contains any missing value.
why: Each fold takes a turn as the test set, so every record is tested once and trained on the rest.
example: A 5-fold study trains on four fifths of the patients and rotates which fifth is held out.
scenario: A small medical set must be tested fully, with each patient used for testing once. Which protocol fits?
scenarioWhy: Rotating the test fold until every patient has been tested once is k-fold cross-validation.

definition: The fraction of positive predictions that are actually positive.
wrongs: The fraction of actual positives that the model successfully finds.
The fraction of all records that receive the correct label.
The average distance from points to their assigned center.
why: Precision looks only at the predicted-positive set and asks how many of those predictions are right.
example: A filter raises 20 spam alerts and 15 of them are truly spam, so precision is 15 out of 20.
scenario: Of 25 fraud alerts, 20 are real fraud. Which metric is 20 divided by 25?
scenarioWhy: The denominator is the number of positive alerts, so the ratio is precision.

definition: The fraction of actual positive records that the model correctly labels positive.
wrongs: The fraction of predicted positives that truly are positive.
The share of itemsets whose confidence exceeds 1.
The number of centers that moved on the last k-means step.
why: Recall uses the actual positives as the denominator and counts how many of them were caught.
example: Among 40 real fraud cases, a detector flags 30, so recall is 30 out of 40.
scenario: A screening test must find as many of the 80 true cases as possible. Which metric tracks that catch rate?
scenarioWhy: Catching actual cases is recall, because the denominator is the set of true positives in the data.

definition: The harmonic mean of precision and recall.
wrongs: The arithmetic mean of training accuracy and test accuracy.
The product of support and confidence for one rule.
The ratio of attributes kept to attributes discarded.
why: The harmonic mean stays high only when both precision and recall are high, so neither error is ignored.
example: A search team reports one number that falls if either relevant hits or found relevant pages become scarce.
scenario: An editor needs a single score that is high only when precision and recall are both high. Which score is appropriate?
scenarioWhy: The harmonic mean of precision and recall is the F1 score.

definition: The fraction of all transactions that contain a given itemset.
wrongs: Among transactions with the antecedent, the fraction that also contain the consequent.
The depth of the deepest leaf in a classification tree.
The distance between two cluster centers.
why: Support counts how often the itemset itself appears, divided by the number of transactions.
example: In 1000 receipts, milk and bread occur together on 200 receipts.
scenario: Milk and bread appear together on 200 of 1000 receipts. Which rule statistic is 200 divided by 1000?
scenarioWhy: The share of all receipts that contain the itemset is support.

definition: Among transactions that contain the antecedent, the fraction that also contain the consequent.
wrongs: The fraction of all transactions that contain both the antecedent and the consequent.
The prior probability of the majority class in the whole training file.
The portion of variance captured by the first principal component.
why: Confidence is a conditional share: it restricts attention to baskets that already contain the antecedent.
example: Among receipts that include cereal, 7 in 10 also include milk.
scenario: Whenever pasta is in a basket, sauce is also there 8 times out of 10. Which statistic is 8 out of 10?
scenarioWhy: The ratio is computed only among baskets that contain pasta, so it is confidence of the rule.

definition: How many times more often the consequent occurs with the antecedent than it occurs by chance.
wrongs: The raw count of transactions that contain an itemset.
The number of folds used when every record is tested once.
The margin width of a separating hyperplane.
why: Lift divides the rule's confidence by the consequent's overall frequency, so 1 means no association beyond chance.
example: Salsa appears with chips four times as often as salsa appears in a random receipt.
scenario: A rule has confidence well above the overall rate of the consequent item. Which statistic shows that extra association?
scenarioWhy: Comparing the conditional rate with the chance rate is what lift measures.

definition: A class-impurity measure that is zero for a pure node and largest when class shares are equal.
wrongs: The count of blank cells in a single column.
The Euclidean distance from a point to the origin.
The percentage of association rules removed after mining.
why: Entropy uses class proportions and reaches zero only when one class occupies the whole node.
example: A node split half yes and half no is more mixed than a node that is entirely yes.
scenario: A leaf contains only the class no. Which impurity measure should be zero for that leaf?
scenarioWhy: A one-class node is pure, so its entropy is zero.

definition: The drop in entropy achieved by splitting a set of records on one chosen attribute.
wrongs: The increase in cluster radius after one more point joins the cluster.
The ratio of test accuracy to training accuracy.
The support of the single most frequent item.
why: Gain subtracts the weighted child entropy from the parent entropy, so a useful split yields a positive drop.
example: Splitting customers on having a premium plan separates churners better than splitting them on shoe size.
scenario: A tree builder compares candidate tests and keeps the one that reduces class impurity the most. Which quantity is being maximized?
scenarioWhy: The impurity drop from a split is information gain.

definition: A classifier that multiplies the class prior by feature likelihoods while assuming features are independent given the class.
wrongs: A clusterer that merges the two closest groups at every step.
A tree that chooses every split by Gini impurity alone.
A miner that ranks rules by lift and ignores class labels.
why: Bayes' rule supplies the class probability, and the naive step factors the joint likelihood into per-feature terms.
example: A spam filter multiplies per-word probabilities and treats words as independent once the spam label is known.
scenario: An email filter scores spam by a class prior times each word likelihood, assuming words are independent given the class. Which classifier is that?
scenarioWhy: A prior times conditionally independent feature likelihoods is the naive Bayes calculation.

definition: A classifier that separates classes using the decision boundary with the widest margin.
wrongs: A method that replaces missing numbers with the column median.
A bar chart of predicted probabilities on the training rows only.
An algorithm that grows a cluster outward from a dense core point.
why: The optimal boundary maximizes the gap to the nearest points of each class, which are the support vectors.
example: A lab model draws the widest street between two classes of tumor measurements in a plane.
scenario: Two diagnosis classes are separable, and the chosen boundary maximizes the gap to the nearest cases. Which classifier is being used?
scenarioWhy: Maximizing the gap between classes is the maximum-margin idea of a support vector machine.

definition: A classifier that labels a new point by the majority class of its k closest training points.
wrongs: A method that maintains k centers and moves each center to its cluster mean.
A tree whose weak branches are removed after a validation check.
A score equal to the harmonic mean of precision and recall.
why: The prediction is a vote of nearby labeled points, and no explicit boundary is stored during training.
example: An unknown flower is labeled by the majority species among the three closest pressed samples.
scenario: A new house is labeled by the majority sale outcome of the 5 closest labeled houses. Which method is that?
scenarioWhy: A majority vote of the nearest labeled neighbors is k-nearest neighbors.

definition: Building a nested tree of clusters by repeatedly merging or splitting groups according to a linkage distance.
wrongs: Assigning every point to one of k fixed centers and updating those centers.
Predicting a numeric bill with a straight-line equation.
Replacing category names with integers that pretend to have order.
why: Each merge or split is kept, so the result is a hierarchy rather than one flat partition.
example: A biologist repeatedly merges the closest species groups until one tree covers all of the animals.
scenario: A taxonomist wants a dendrogram of species, merging the closest groups step by step. Which clustering style is that?
scenarioWhy: Successive merges recorded as a tree are hierarchical clustering.

definition: A density-based clusterer that grows clusters from core points and marks sparse points as noise.
wrongs: A method that requires the user to choose k and represents each cluster by its mean.
A supervised model that outputs class probabilities from a prior and likelihoods.
A table used only to derive precision and recall.
why: Membership follows density reachability from core points, so arbitrary shapes and noise points are allowed.
example: A city map of crashes forms dense street clusters and leaves isolated rural crashes marked as noise.
scenario: Accident points form irregular dense blobs, and isolated points should be called noise without choosing k. Which clusterer fits?
scenarioWhy: Density reachability with noise points and no preset k is DBSCAN.

definition: A score from -1 to 1 that is high when a point is much closer to its own cluster than to the next cluster.
wrongs: The fraction of test records that received the correct class label.
The minimum support required to keep an itemset.
The count of attributes remaining after selection.
why: The score compares a point's average distance inside its cluster with its average distance to the nearest other cluster.
example: A shopper near the middle of one segment and far from the next segment receives a score close to 1.
scenario: After clustering stores, an analyst wants a -1 to 1 score of how well each store sits in its own group. Which score is that?
scenarioWhy: A cohesion-versus-separation score on that range is the silhouette coefficient.

definition: The labeled records used to fit a model's parameters or structure.
wrongs: The records held aside solely to estimate final performance.
The unlabeled batch scored after the model is deployed.
The list of attributes removed as irrelevant.
why: Fitting uses these records to set splits, weights, or probabilities before any final test.
example: Eight thousand labeled product reviews are used to fit a sentiment classifier.
scenario: A model adjusts its splits using 7000 labeled tickets and does not use the other 3000 for fitting. What are the 7000 tickets called?
scenarioWhy: Records used to fit the model are the training set.

definition: Labeled records withheld from training and used to estimate performance on new data.
wrongs: The records whose errors are used to update the model during fitting.
The product list used to count how often an item is bought.
The centers produced by the first k-means iteration.
why: Because the model never fit these labels, their errors estimate generalization.
example: Two thousand labeled reviews that were never used in fitting provide the published accuracy.
scenario: A team freezes a model, then scores it once on 1500 labeled customers never seen in fitting. What is that group of customers?
scenarioWrongs: The validation fold used to grow the tree
scenarioWhy: Labeled rows withheld from fitting and used for a performance estimate form the test set.

definition: A single split of labeled data into a training portion and a separate test portion.
wrongs: Several rotated splits in which every record is tested exactly once.
A bootstrap sample drawn with replacement to train each tree in a forest.
A projection of all columns onto two variance-maximizing axes.
why: Holdout performs one partition into train and test rather than rotating several folds.
example: A class randomly assigns 70 percent of rows to training and 30 percent to testing one time.
scenario: Students split a labeled file once into 80 percent for fitting and 20 percent for a final score. Which protocol is that?
scenarioWhy: One train-test cut, without rotating folds, is the holdout method.

definition: Scaling a numeric attribute into a fixed range, often 0 to 1, using its minimum and maximum.
wrongs: Subtracting the mean and dividing by the standard deviation.
Replacing each category with several orthogonal binary columns.
Cutting a continuous attribute into equal-width bins.
why: The minimum maps to the low end of the range and the maximum maps to the high end, with values scaled linearly between them.
example: Ages from 0 to 100 are mapped onto 0 to 1 before a distance-based classifier runs.
scenario: Income must be mapped onto 0 to 1 using the smallest and largest incomes in the column. Which scaling is that?
scenarioWhy: Using the column minimum and maximum to reach a fixed range is min-max normalization.

definition: Rescaling a numeric attribute so that its mean is 0 and its standard deviation is 1.
wrongs: Mapping every value linearly onto 0 to 1 using the minimum and maximum.
Replacing extreme points with the nearest boxplot whisker.
Splitting a date into separate year, month, and day columns.
why: Subtracting the mean centers the column at 0, and dividing by the standard deviation sets the spread to 1.
example: Household incomes are recentered and rescaled until the column has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
scenario: A distance model needs each numeric column to have mean 0 and standard deviation 1. Which transform applies?
scenarioWhy: Centering by the mean and scaling by the standard deviation produces z-scores.

definition: Filling absent entries with estimated values such as a mean, median, mode, or model prediction.
wrongs: Deleting every column that stores any numeric measurement.
Assigning a random class label to rows that already have labels.
Sorting the file so blank cells fall at the bottom and then ignoring them in reports only.
why: Imputation puts a substitute value into an empty cell so the row can remain in the analysis.
example: Blank salary cells in a hiring file are replaced with the median salary of that column.
scenario: A census column is missing on some forms, and those cells are replaced by the column median. Which operation is that?
scenarioWhy: Substituting an estimate for an absent entry is imputation.

definition: A record whose values lie unusually far from the bulk of the data and may distort a model.
wrongs: The most frequent class in a labeled training set.
A leaf that contains exactly one training record of the majority class.
An item that appears in every transaction in the log.
why: The record is extreme relative to the rest of the sample, so means, distances, or splits can be pulled toward it.
example: One invoice of 900000 dollars sits far above a column whose typical bill is near 40 dollars.
scenario: Among apartment rents clustered near 1200 dollars, one recorded rent is 25 million dollars. What is that record called?
scenarioWhy: A value that far from the bulk of the rents is an outlier.

definition: Converting a continuous attribute into a small number of ordered bins or intervals.
wrongs: Scaling a column to mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
Expanding one category into several binary indicator columns.
Dropping attributes whose correlation with the label is high.
why: Each numeric value is replaced by the interval that contains it, so the attribute becomes categorical and ordered.
example: Age is placed into child, teen, adult, and senior bins before association rules are mined.
scenario: A rule miner needs age as young, mid, or senior rather than as a raw number of years. Which transform is required?
scenarioWhy: Replacing a continuous age with ordered intervals is discretization.

definition: Representing a categorical attribute as binary columns, one per category, with a single 1 in the active column.
wrongs: Replacing each category by an integer rank from 1 through the number of levels.
Splitting a numeric column at its median into two bins.
Hashing every text field into one shared numeric identifier.
why: Each category gets its own column, so the coding does not invent a false numeric order among categories.
example: A color field with values red, green, and blue becomes three yes-or-no columns.
scenario: City names must enter a distance model without implying that one city code is greater than another. Which encoding avoids that false order?
scenarioWhy: Separate binary columns do not place the cities on a numeric scale.

definition: Representing records with fewer attributes while keeping as much useful structure as possible.
wrongs: Adding an interaction column for every pair of original attributes.
Copying minority-class rows until the class counts match.
Growing a tree until every training leaf is pure.
why: The transformed records use fewer coordinates, but the kept coordinates are chosen to preserve variation or class structure.
example: Face photos of 10000 pixels are represented with 50 components before clustering identities.
scenario: A spreadsheet of 500 correlated sensor channels must be analyzed with far fewer columns. Which goal is that?
scenarioWhy: Replacing many channels with a smaller set of informative coordinates reduces dimension.

definition: An unsupervised transform that builds uncorrelated axes ordered by how much variance they capture.
wrongs: A supervised ranking of attributes by chi-square association with the class label.
A clustering step that sets k equal to the number of known classes.
A filter that keeps only association rules whose lift is above 1.
why: Each next component is orthogonal to the earlier ones and captures as much remaining variance as possible.
example: Answers to 40 correlated survey items are rotated into uncorrelated axes ordered by captured variance.
scenario: A scientist wants new uncorrelated coordinates that successively capture the most variance, with no class label used. Which method applies?
scenarioWhy: Unsupervised variance-ordered orthogonal axes are principal components.

definition: Using a model too weak to capture the real pattern, so error stays high on both training and new data.
wrongs: Memorizing training quirks so that new records are predicted poorly.
Building a tree whose every leaf contains only one class.
Obtaining a clustering whose silhouette scores are close to 1.
why: The model class cannot represent the signal, so even the training error remains large.
example: A classifier that always predicts the majority class misses the real pattern on both the fit data and later data.
scenario: Both training error and test error stay near the majority-class baseline for a very shallow model. Which problem is present?
scenarioWhy: High error on the training data as well as on new data indicates underfitting.

definition: The balance between a model's systematic error and its sensitivity to the particular training sample.
wrongs: The choice between precision and recall when the positive class is rare.
The gap between support and confidence of one association rule.
The choice between Euclidean distance and Manhattan distance.
why: Simpler models tend to have higher bias and lower variance, while more flexible models do the reverse.
example: A very deep tree changes wildly when the training sample changes, while a one-level stump stays stable but crude.
scenario: Making a model more flexible cuts systematic error but makes predictions jump when the training sample changes. Which tradeoff is that?
scenarioWhy: Systematic error is bias and sample sensitivity is variance, so the described balance is that tradeoff.

definition: A plot of true-positive rate against false-positive rate as the decision threshold changes.
wrongs: A plot of training loss against the number of passes through the training file.
A bar chart of how many records belong to each class in the raw file.
A tree diagram of merge distances from hierarchical clustering.
why: Each threshold gives one true-positive rate and one false-positive rate, and those pairs trace the curve.
example: Lowering an alert cutoff traces how the catch rate rises together with the false-alarm rate.
scenario: A bank plots catch rate against false-alarm rate while sliding the fraud score cutoff. Which plot is produced?
scenarioWhy: True-positive rate versus false-positive rate across thresholds is an ROC curve.

definition: The area under the ROC curve, summarizing ranking quality across all decision thresholds.
wrongs: The accuracy obtained at one chosen probability cutoff.
The height of the tallest bar in a class-count histogram.
The number of true negatives in one confusion matrix.
why: Integrating the ROC curve rewards a model that ranks positives above negatives across thresholds, not at one cutoff.
example: Two churn models are compared by the area under their ROC curves rather than by one operating point.
scenario: A clinic wants one number for a score's ranking quality over every cutoff, not accuracy at a single cutoff. Which number fits?
scenarioWhy: Area under the ROC curve summarizes performance across all thresholds.

definition: An actual positive record that the classifier also predicts as positive.
wrongs: An actual negative record that the classifier predicts as positive.
An actual positive record that the classifier predicts as negative.
An actual negative record that the classifier predicts as negative.
why: Both the true label and the predicted label are positive, so the prediction is a hit on a positive case.
example: A biopsy that truly shows cancer is also marked cancer by the screening model.
scenario: A message is spam and the filter also labels it spam. Which confusion-matrix outcome is that?
scenarioWhy: A real positive that is predicted positive is a true positive.

definition: Learning a mapping from inputs to a known target by using examples that already include that target.
wrongs: Searching for groups in records that were collected without a target label.
Discovering which products are bought together without using a class label.
Compressing attributes into fewer coordinates without predicting an output.
why: The training examples include the target, so the learner can compare predictions with known answers.
example: Sale prices already printed on past deeds are used to learn how features of a house relate to price.
scenario: Historic loans include a default flag, and a model learns to predict that flag for new applicants. Which learning style is this?
scenarioWhy: The default flag is a known target on the training loans, so learning is supervised.

definition: Finding structure such as clusters or dense regions when no target label is given.
wrongs: Fitting a classifier on examples whose class label is already known.
Estimating accuracy with a labeled holdout set.
Choosing the attribute split that most reduces class entropy.
why: Without a target, the algorithm can only use similarities or densities among the inputs.
example: Machine-sensor traces are grouped into operating regimes even though no failure label was recorded.
scenario: Web logs have no topic labels, and an analyst groups sessions by similarity. Which learning style is that?
scenarioWhy: Grouping inputs with no target label is unsupervised learning.

definition: A frequent-itemset method that extends a set only when every one of its subsets is already frequent.
wrongs: A clustering loop that replaces each center with the mean of its assigned points.
A split rule that always chooses the attribute with the lowest Gini impurity.
A kernel method that maximizes the margin between two classes.
why: If a subset is infrequent, every larger set containing it is infrequent, so those candidates are pruned.
example: Candidate pairs are discarded as soon as either item alone falls below the minimum support.
scenario: A retailer drops any pair whose individual items are already below minimum support, then builds longer sets only from frequent pieces. Which algorithm is that?
scenarioWhy: Pruning candidates by the frequent-subset property is the Apriori step.

definition: A split score that is zero for a pure node and higher when class proportions are more evenly mixed.
wrongs: The fraction of transactions that contain a chosen itemset.
The width of the margin around a separating hyperplane.
The silhouette of one point's cluster assignment.
why: Gini impurity is computed from class proportions and vanishes only when a single class fills the node.
example: A node that is 90 percent one class has lower Gini impurity than a node split 50-50.
scenario: A tree algorithm compares splits using an impurity that is zero in a pure node and based on squared class shares. Which impurity is that?
scenarioWhy: An impurity of zero for a pure node that uses class-share squares is Gini impurity.

definition: Removing branches from a grown tree so the tree overfits less and predicts new records better.
wrongs: Adding attributes until every training leaf contains only one class.
Increasing k until every point is its own cluster.
Lowering minimum support until nearly every itemset is kept.
why: Branches that fit training noise are cut, which usually lowers error on data the tree did not fit.
example: Branches that fail to improve validation accuracy are cut from a fully grown admissions tree.
scenario: A fully grown tree is perfect on training rows, so branches that hurt a validation set are removed. Which remedy is that?
scenarioWrongs: Raising k to the sample size
scenarioWhy: Cutting branches that do not help unseen rows is pruning.

definition: Combining several models so their joint prediction is more stable than any one of the models.
wrongs: Keeping only the single attribute with the highest correlation to the label.
Replacing the model with a prediction of the majority class for every row.
Stopping when training accuracy first reaches 100 percent.
why: Errors that differ across members can cancel when the members vote or average their predictions.
example: Five default models vote on each applicant, and the majority vote is the decision that is stored.
scenario: A team averages the class probabilities of several different models instead of trusting one model. Which approach is that?
scenarioWhy: Combining several models' predictions is an ensemble method.

definition: An ensemble of decision trees, each trained on a bootstrap sample and a random subset of attributes at each split.
wrongs: One unpruned tree that tests every attribute in order at the root.
A Bayes classifier that assumes features are independent given the class.
A density clusterer that requires a neighborhood radius and a core-point count.
why: Bootstrap samples and random attribute subsets make the trees differ, and their votes form the forest prediction.
example: One hundred trees each see a bootstrap of patients and a random handful of lab tests, then the trees vote.
scenario: Many trees are grown on bootstrap samples with a random subset of features at each split, and they vote. Which model is that?
scenarioWhy: Bootstrap trees plus random feature subsets and a vote define a random forest.

definition: Mining retail transactions to find items that customers tend to purchase together.
wrongs: Forecasting tomorrow's total store revenue from a daily sales time series.
Grouping stores by floor area and number of employees.
Labeling product reviews as positive or negative sentiment.
why: Each transaction is a basket, and the analysis looks for co-occurring items rather than a class label.
example: A supermarket mines receipts and then places chips on the shelf beside salsa.
scenario: A grocer wants product pairs that show up in the same receipt so the pairs can share an endcap. Which analysis is that?
scenarioWhy: Finding products bought in the same receipt is market basket analysis.

definition: Detecting and repairing errors, duplicates, and inconsistent codes in records before analysis.
wrongs: Scoring a deployed model on live traffic that has no labels yet.
Drawing an ROC curve after the classifier has already been trained.
Choosing k from the elbow of a within-cluster distance plot.
why: Cleaning fixes what is wrong or duplicated in the records themselves, before transforms or models run.
example: Duplicate patient identifiers are merged, and impossible ages such as 400 are corrected.
scenario: Two rows share one student id, and a birth year of 3021 appears in the file. Which task addresses both problems?
